newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd's sets date for revised electronic system.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's sets date for revised electronic system.

text.p: Lloyds of London will on April 7 launch a simplified version of the controversial electronic placing support (EPS) system, insurance market sources told Reuters on Thursday.
EPS Support is limited to creating an electronic record once an insurance risk has been underwritten, making it much more market friendly than the complete EPS system.
"With EPS, brokers and underwriters have to keep updating their records electronically throughout negotiations. For complex risks this is a nightmare," one market source said.
The new, slimmed down EPS Support, which has been tested by around 30 underwriters, means that negotiations take place in the traditional way using paper, rather than electronic records.
"This amounts to a semi-relaunch of EPS," said another insurance source.
EPS has met with limited enthusiasm since its launch in the early 1990s, despite being intended to reduce costs and create common core records to cut down the amount of information that is re-keyed.
After many missed deadlines, last year saw the removal of targets for usage of EPS, which was designed for all participants in the London insurance market.

Recently, however, insurers have shown more willingness to embrace the principle of electronic systems to support their business, although they remain critical of their current drawbacks and complexities.
Earlier this week, London-based aviation insurers said they were ready to start doing business electronically, but added that systems for trading insurance on computer screens did not yet exist.

"We're equipped and have trained underwriters ready to do it," Keith Selby, head of aviation underwriting at Swiss Re in London, told a news conference before the annual meeting of the Aviation Insurance Officers Association.

The current EPS system was not particularly suited to complex aviation risks, he said, while the World Insurance Network (WIN) being developed by leading brokers did not yet have business applications.
"WIN (World Insurance Network) is one possibility, but at the moment it's designed to be a communications network," he added.
"I'm not saying we want huge applications. We want simple solutions that speed things up and make them cheaper," he told Reuters.
